title: Global Mental Health Just Hit Its Lowest Recorded Level. The Diaspora's Silence Makes It Worse.
excerpt: The 2026 AXA Mind Health Report surveyed 19,000 adults across 18 countries and found 46 per cent are languishing or struggling. Among younger generations, that number is 59 per cent. South Asian Americans remain among the least likely to seek help — and the most likely to turn to AI chatbots instead.
body:
The numbers arrived quietly in early June, buried under geopolitical headlines and market volatility. AXA and Ipsos released the sixth edition of the Mind Health Report, the largest annual global survey of psychological well-being. The headline finding is stark: mental health across the world has reached its lowest point since the study began tracking it.

Nearly half of the 19,000 adults surveyed across 18 countries — 46 per cent — are either languishing or actively struggling. Among younger adults, the figure climbs to 59 per cent. And one of the most striking data points is not about how people feel, but how they cope: 61 per cent of respondents have already used artificial intelligence tools for mental health support.

## Five Hours a Day, and Two-Thirds Know It Is Hurting Them

The report identifies a pattern that anyone with a smartphone will recognise. The average adult now spends 5.1 hours per day on screens outside of work — scrolling, consuming, reacting. Two-thirds of respondents acknowledged that this habit has a negative impact on their daily lives.

A parallel study published in *Nature*, analysing over 50,000 American children and adolescents, found that more than four hours of daily screen time was associated with higher risks of anxiety, depression, behavioural problems, and ADHD. Physical activity reduction accounted for 31 to 39 per cent of that association. Irregular bedtimes accounted for another 18 to 24 per cent.

The mechanism is not mysterious. Screen time displaces movement. Movement regulates mood. Irregular light exposure disrupts circadian rhythm. Disrupted sleep amplifies anxiety. The cycle is self-reinforcing and, for the generation that grew up with smartphones, feels entirely normal — which is precisely what makes it dangerous.

## The South Asian Silence

For Indian Americans and the broader South Asian diaspora, these global numbers land on a community uniquely ill-equipped to respond to them.

Asian Americans use anxiety medication at roughly half the rate of white Americans. A 2025 study found this disparity persists even after controlling for income, insurance, and access to care. The gap is not about availability. It is about perception.

In South Asian households, mental health struggles still carry a vocabulary problem. Depression is often reframed as laziness. Anxiety is called overthinking. Therapy is something other people need. The model minority narrative — the idea that South Asians in America are educated, successful, and therefore fine — creates a ceiling on how much suffering the community is permitted to acknowledge.

The AXA report's finding that one-third of people who do not seek professional help believe their situation is not serious enough mirrors this dynamic almost perfectly. When your culture tells you that struggling is a character flaw, you are unlikely to classify your own distress as clinical.

## The AI Therapy Paradox

Perhaps the most revealing data point is the 61 per cent who have turned to AI for mental health support. Usage is highest in China, the Philippines, and Turkey — countries where therapy is either stigmatised, expensive, or both.

For diaspora communities, AI chatbots offer something traditional therapy does not: anonymity. There is no appointment to explain to your parents. No name on a therapist's intake form. No risk that someone from the temple or the desi WhatsApp group will see your car in the clinic parking lot.

But the report also reveals the limits. Twenty-eight per cent of people who followed AI-generated mental health advice reported harmful outcomes. Only 38 per cent trust AI more than a human professional. Thirty-two per cent said they felt uncomfortable with the advice they received.

AI can open a door. It cannot do therapy. The distinction matters enormously when the person on the other side of the screen has never spoken to a therapist and has no framework for evaluating what good care looks like.

## What the Diaspora Needs to Hear

The AXA report identifies self-acceptance as the single most important skill for moving from languishing to flourishing. This finding is worth sitting with, because self-acceptance is precisely what the model minority framework makes hardest.

Accepting that you are struggling requires letting go of the narrative that you are supposed to have it figured out. For first-generation immigrants who sacrificed everything for opportunity, admitting to mental health difficulties can feel like betraying the premise of the migration itself. For second-generation kids, it means acknowledging that the American dream they were handed came with costs that were never part of the brochure.

None of this is weakness. The AXA data shows it is a global crisis, not a personal failure. Nearly six in ten young people worldwide are struggling, regardless of nationality, income, or education level.

The difference is whether your community gives you permission to say so.

## What Actually Helps

The research points to interventions that do not require a therapist's couch or a prescription pad. Physical activity — even 30 minutes of walking — was the single strongest mediator between screen time and mental health outcomes in the *Nature* study. Regular bedtimes mattered more than total sleep duration. Reducing non-work screen time by even one hour per day shifted outcomes measurably.

For South Asian families, the most powerful intervention may be the simplest: normalising the conversation. Asking your teenager how they are feeling — and meaning it. Telling your parents that you see a therapist — and not apologising for it. Recognising that the uncle who sits alone at every family gathering might not be antisocial. He might be depressed.

The 2026 data is clear. The problem is not that people do not know they are struggling. It is that they have been told it does not count.

Sources: AXA / Ipsos 2026 Mind Health Report, *Nature*, *Contemporary Pediatrics*, *JAMA Network Open*
